notes.meaning: The Lord gave Ezekiel another message to deliver to the exiles in Babylon. God used the story of two sisters to explain the history and sins of His people.

God describes two women who were daughters of the same mother. These two sisters represent the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah, who came from the same family line through Abraham and Sarah.

Early in their history, while living in Egypt, the Israelites turned away from God and worshiped false idols. God describes this unfaithfulness as a young woman giving herself to lovers before marriage.

The older sister is named Oholah, which means 'her tent,' standing for Samaria and her self-made shrines. The younger sister is Oholibah, meaning 'my tent is in her,' standing for Jerusalem, where God placed His holy temple. Both belonged to the Lord in a sacred marriage agreement, yet both chose to be unfaithful.

Even while Samaria was joined to the Lord, she looked away to foreign nations for safety. She chased after the powerful Assyrian empire, longing for their friendship and adopting their wicked practices.

The leaders of Samaria were charmed by the fine purple clothing, high ranks, and strong cavalry of Assyrian warriors. Instead of trusting God to defend them, they were dazzled by human power and worldly splendor.
Samaria gave herself completely to Assyria by worshiping all their false gods. Seeking security in worldly powers led God's people straight into the filth of foreign idolatry.
The northern kingdom never abandoned the false calf worship she had learned in Egypt centuries earlier. Instead of giving up old sins, she simply added new Assyrian idols to her unfaithfulness.
Because Samaria refused to be faithful, God handed her over to the very Assyrian empire she had trusted. The worldly powers that sinners run to often become the instruments of their destruction.

The Assyrians stripped Samaria of her wealth, captured her children, and destroyed the nation with the sword in 722 BC. Samaria became an infamous warning to all surrounding nations about the cost of abandoning God.
Jerusalem saw the total ruin of her sister kingdom, but she did not take the warning to heart. Instead, Judah pursued foreign alliances and idols even more recklessly than Samaria had.
Judah was just as fascinated by the splendidly dressed Assyrian officers and their powerful cavalry. Kings like Ahaz made treaties with Assyria and even copied their pagan altars inside Jerusalem.
The Lord saw that Judah was polluted with the exact same sins as Israel. Both kingdoms abandoned their true Protector to chase after human strength and foreign gods.

Jerusalem went even further by falling in love with carvings and bright red paintings of Babylonian soldiers. These pictures showed great military officers wearing dyed turbans and handsome belts. Judah was drawn into idolatry merely by gazing at images of foreign power and prestige.
As soon as Judah saw these portraits, she sent messengers all the way to Chaldea to secure a partnership. Sin often enters through the eyes and drives people to seek safety outside of God.

The Babylonians formed an alliance with Judah and brought their false worship into the land. But after a time, Judah grew tired of Babylonian rule and turned away, looking for new partners to help her rebel.
When Jerusalem acted so openly and shamelessly in her unfaithfulness, the Lord turned away from her in disgust. He rejected Judah just as He had rejected her sister Samaria years earlier.
Instead of turning back to God, Jerusalem doubled down on her unfaithfulness. She fondly remembered the days of her youth in Egypt and reached back out to Egypt for military help against Babylon.

God uses shocking, crude imagery of animal lust to describe how desperately Judah chased after Egypt's army. The blunt language shows how repulsive and shameful it is for God's covenant people to depend on pagan nations.
Jerusalem eagerly repeated the disgraceful idolatry and reliance on Egypt that had begun in her earliest days. By reviving those ancient sins, she ensured that God's judgment would fall upon her.

Because Judah broke her treaties, the Lord announced that He would bring her former Babylonian allies against her as enemies. The very armies Jerusalem had once courted would surround the city on every side.

Babylon would march with a coalition of Chaldean warriors, troops from Pekod, Shoa, and Koa, and Assyrian forces. All of these horsemen and famous commanders would unite to execute God's sentence against Judah.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: In the Latin Vulgate tradition, Jerome understood Pekod, Shoa, and Koa as titles of noble ranks or officers rather than names of regions and tribes.

notes.meaning: This massive army would surround Jerusalem with chariots, supply wagons, shields, and helmets. God would place Judah into their hands to be judged according to the brutal customs and laws of Babylon.
